# Structural Beat Sheet: "The Reykjavik Frequency Heist"
## Three Essential Beats

---

## Beat 1: The Signal as Magnús's Annoyance — Establishing Dual-Timeline Skepticism

**Concrete Action (1971):** Magnús, a methodical radio engineer comfortable with knowable waveforms, is recruited by the physicist Elísabet Jónsdóttir to help capture an anomalous signal emanating from the Krafla volcanic system. He agrees not because he believes the signal contains future broadcasts — he considers this flatly insane — but because the *technical* problem intrigues him: the signal is real, measurably there, conforming to no known transmission pattern, and isolating it represents a genuine engineering puzzle. Elísabet assembles a team of misfits. Equipment is scavenged from decommissioned fishing trawlers. Plans are drawn up to bribe a Soviet monitoring station for access to restricted frequencies. Magnús narrates all of this with the dry, slightly superior tone of a man who believes he is the only adult in the room.

**(2019):** An elderly Magnús sits across from his interviewer — or his camera, or his grandchild, whoever the frame's audience surrogate is — and the very first thing he establishes is that Elísabet was *right.* He says this flatly, without fanfare, before any context has been provided. The 2019 frame opens with the conclusion. Then it reverses into the beginning.

**Narrative Technique:** *The unreliable framing narrator who is unreliable in opposite directions across two timelines.* In 1971, Magnús's skepticism is the reader's entry point and feels rational, trustworthy, even comforting. He catalogs Elísabet's flaws — her arrogance, her emasculating dismissals of his caution, her tendency to treat physics as revelation rather than measurement. The reader bonds with Magnús because he is the empiricist, the proceduralist, the one who double-checks the wiring. But the 2019 frame has already told us his skepticism was wrong. This means every scene of Magnús condescending to Elísabet is quietly dramatic irony: *we* know she was right; *he* didn't yet. The reader occupies a strange double consciousness — siding with him emotionally in 1971 while knowing intellectually from 2019 that his entire interpretive framework is inadequate. This split is the engine of the story's tension long before any heist mechanics generate their own suspense.

The docudrama register matters here. Present the 1971 material with the texture of meticulous reconstruction — timestamps, equipment model numbers, weather conditions, the specific frequency ranges Magnús tested. Let Magnús's engineering voice seduce the reader into treating this as a procedural about eccentric Cold War–era radio hobbyists. The more grounded and technically credible the 1971 voice is, the more devastating the eventual confirmation of the impossible will be. The genre itself becomes the misdirection: the reader trusts docudrama conventions to keep them in the realm of the explainable.

**What Makes It Essential:** This beat must accomplish three things simultaneously: (1) make Magnús's competence and skepticism feel genuinely authoritative so the reader adopts his lens, (2) make Elísabet's brilliance visible *through* Magnús's irritation with her — he must inadvertently reveal that she is extraordinary even as he catalogs her impossibility, and (3) establish the 2019 frame's gravitational pull. The elderly Magnús knows something that cost him, and the reader must feel the weight of 48 years of silence pressing on every sentence he speaks. Not melodramatically. Not with trembling hands and long pauses. With the specific weight of a man who has rehearsed what he will say and is now, finally, saying it, and it still isn't coming out the way he planned.

Elísabet's characterization must be constructed entirely through Magnús's filtered perception, which means the reader has to learn to read against his narration. When he describes her "relentless emasculation of his cautious engineering instincts," the text should make clear — without Magnús realizing it — that what she was actually doing was pushing past the limitations of his imagination. His word for her was *impossible.* Her word for him, which he quotes with residual sting decades later, should be something more precise and more wounding — something that names the specific smallness of a man who only believes in what his instruments have already measured.

**Structural Choice That Must Work:** The 2019 opening concession — *she was right* — is the story's equivalent of the grandmother's clothing chosen for her own corpse. It tells the reader exactly what will happen, in plain language, and the reader absorbs it without feeling its full weight. In O'Connor, the grandmother dresses for death before page two; here, Magnús confesses the impossible was real before the first piece of trawler equipment is unboxed. Both techniques work by exploiting the reader's assumption that *knowing the destination* is the same as *understanding the journey.* It isn't. The entire story exists in that gap.

The bribery of the Soviet monitoring station should be introduced here as a procedural complication — logistically tense, narratively engaging — but it also seeds something crucial: other people were listening to these frequencies. Other institutions knew the signal existed. The team is not discovering something hidden. They are *stealing* something guarded. That distinction must be legible from the start, even if its full implications don't land until Beat 2.

---

## Beat 2: The Signal Resolves — Procedural Success Becomes Moral Catastrophe

**Concrete Action (1971):** Through a prolonged sequence of technical problem-solving — each obstacle a satisfying procedural set piece in itself — the team succeeds in isolating and capturing the Krafla signal. Magnús's engineering is what makes it work; the repurposed trawler equipment, tuned with his particular genius for coaxing fidelity from junk hardware, finally locks onto the frequency with clarity. This is his professional triumph. And then they listen. And the signal is exactly what Elísabet said it was.

The content resolves in layers. First, what sounds like static reveals fragments of Icelandic-language news broadcasts. Then dates become legible — dates that haven't happened yet. Then specific events. Each layer of clarity that Magnús's engineering extracts is another layer of the impossible confirmed, and each confirmation peels away one more wall of his skepticism until he is standing in the open with no framework left. The procedural victories that structured the first half of the story — each technical problem solved feeling like progress toward a goal — now reveal themselves as steps deeper into something the team was not prepared to confront.

The critical turn: among the future broadcasts, certain predictions are not merely strange but *specific and catastrophic.* The story should not reveal all of them at once. It should let Magnús describe, from 2019, the experience of hearing fragments — and then going quiet about certain fragments. The 2019 Magnús edits. He hesitates. He describes around the edges. The reader must feel the shape of what he won't say before he says it.

Elísabet's reaction to the confirmed signal is not triumph. It is not vindication. This is the moment that redefines her in Magnús's eyes and in ours. She listens, she verifies, and then she becomes very still, and she begins asking Magnús technical questions — not about how to preserve the signal but about its *architecture.* How is it structured? Is it a loop? Is it complete? Can it be isolated to specific date ranges? Magnús, still reeling from the ontological shock of the signal being real, doesn't understand why she's asking engineering questions instead of celebrating. He gives her the answers. He does not yet realize he is giving her what she needs to destroy it.

**(2019):** Elderly Magnús describes the moment he understood the signal was real as the moment his life broke into *before* and *after*. But he describes it with a specific, engineering-precise grief: it wasn't the impossibility that broke him. It was that his instruments confirmed it. His own tools, his own careful calibrations, his own professional expertise — the very things that had made him feel superior to Elísabet — became the proof that she was right and his entire model of the world was wrong. His competence betrayed him into knowledge. This is the inversion of his role: the skeptic's skill set becomes the mechanism of his own undoing.

**Narrative Technique:** *Procedural structure weaponized against the reader's genre expectations.* For the first half of the story, each solved technical problem delivers the satisfying dopamine of heist-narrative progress: they get the equipment, they get the frequency access, they tune the signal, they beat the clock. The reader is trained by genre to feel that solving problems = approaching victory. Beat 2 maintains the procedural texture — Magnús is still describing technical work, still narrating in his competent engineer's voice — but the *meaning* of success inverts entirely. Solving the signal doesn't unlock a prize. It unlocks a burden. The same narrative mechanism (problem → solution → new problem) continues, but "new problem" has shifted from *how do we capture the signal* to *what do we do with the knowledge that the future is audible and contains horrors.*

The intercut structure between timelines should tighten here. Shorter jumps. The 1971 Magnús solving a wiring problem, cut against the 2019 Magnús going silent for a beat too long. The technical and the emotional braiding together until they become one texture. The reader should feel the 2019 silences as pressure — what is he not saying? — while the 1971 sequences provide the literal content he's circling around.

Elísabet's questions about the signal's architecture should read, on first pass, as scientific rigor. She is a physicist; of course she wants to understand the signal's structure. Only in retrospect — or on a second reading — does the reader realize she was already planning what she would do. She was not studying the signal. She was *casing* it. The heist-within-the-heist: she stole the signal from the airwaves, yes, but her real operation was stealing the team's moment of triumph and converting it into an act of destruction. The first heist was procedural. The second heist is moral, and Magnús was her unwitting accomplice in both.

**What Makes It Essential:** This beat is the structural hinge — the equivalent of O'Connor's car accident. It is the moment where genre flips. What was a Cold War procedural becomes an ethical nightmare. What was a heist becomes a question: *If you could hear tomorrow's catastrophes, would knowing them make you responsible for them?* And beneath that: *What if the signal's existence itself — the possibility that someone could listen, could intervene, could exploit — is the catastrophe?*

The key emotional revelation in this beat is not the signal's content. It is the change in the relationship between Magnús and Elísabet. All through Beat 1, he condescended to her. Here, in the moment of confirmation, the power dynamic doesn't simply reverse (that would be too neat, too satisfying). Instead, it *collapses.* They are both lost. She is not triumphant and he is not humbled. They are two people standing inside an impossible fact, and for one brief stretch — which the 2019 Magnús describes with the most tender and complicated language in the whole story — they are equals in their terror. That equality is what he has spent 48 years unable to talk about. Not the signal. Not the future. The fact that for a few hours in 1971, a woman he had spent weeks underestimating became the only person in the world who understood what he was feeling, and he became the only person who understood her, and what they built in that understanding was the decision to destroy everything they had accomplished.

**Structural Choice That Must Work:** The layered revelation of the signal's content must be paced like the peeling of an onion — each layer more specific, more verifiable, more terrible. But the story should withold the *specific catastrophic prediction* that triggers Elísabet's decision until Beat 3. Here, we see her *react* to it. We see her go quiet. We see her begin asking the questions. We feel the weight. But we do not yet know the specific content. This is the narrative equivalent of O'Connor's offstage gunshots: the reader hears the report but does not witness the death. The imagination fills in something worse than any specific detail could provide — and when Beat 3 finally reveals the specific content, it should be both surprising and *less* than what the reader imagined, because what matters is not the prediction itself but Elísabet's decision about it. The content is the MacGuffin. The choice is the story.

---

## Beat 3: The Destruction and the Confession — "Stealing Tomorrow" Means Refusing It

**Concrete Action (1971):** Hours before Icelandic government forces (alerted, we now learn, by the Soviets whose monitoring station was bribed — that procedural detail from Beat 1 converting from texture into consequence) close in on the team's location, Elísabet tells Magnús they must destroy the captured signal. Not hide it. Not encrypt it. Destroy it — the recordings, the equipment calibrations that would allow recapture, Magnús's own meticulously kept engineering logs. Everything. Magnús resists. This is his work. This is *proof of the impossible.* This is the most significant technical achievement of his life. And she is asking him to be the one to unmake it, because only he has the technical knowledge to do it thoroughly.

The argument between them is the scene the entire story has been building toward. Not the heist. Not the signal. This. Elísabet finally articulates what she understood the moment the signal resolved and Magnús did not: the signal's specific predictions included not just catastrophes but the *responses* to those catastrophes — and the responses were warped by foreknowledge. Someone, in some timeline or some reality adjacent to this one, *had* the signal, and acted on it, and the acting-on-it produced something worse than the original events. The signal was not a warning. It was a record of what happens when people *use* warnings. The future it broadcast was not the future that would happen without intervention. It was the future that happened *because of* intervention. Elísabet's phrase — "stealing tomorrow" — reveals its actual meaning: she isn't stealing the future *for* them. She is stealing it *away from* them. She is removing the temptation to act on knowledge that, by its very nature, poisons every action it informs.

Magnús destroys everything. He describes, from 2019, the technical process of destruction with the same meticulous specificity he used to describe the process of construction. The parallel is deliberate and devastating: the same expertise, the same careful hands, the same engineering precision — applied in reverse. He unmakes his masterwork, and he does it well, because he is very good at his job.

The government forces arrive and find nothing. The team scatters. Elísabet disappears from Magnús's life — not dramatically, not with a final confrontation, but gradually, the way people lose each other when the thing that joined them is gone, and what remains is only the shared knowledge of what they did, which is exactly the kind of knowledge
narrative_story:
# The Reykjavik Frequency Heist

---

## I.

She was right.

I want to say that first, before any of the rest of it, because I spent the better part of 1971 constructing an elaborate interior argument for why she was wrong, and I have spent the forty-eight years since then living inside the knowledge that she was not, and if I begin this story the way I lived it — with my own confident skepticism as the scaffolding — then I will be lying to you in the specific way I spent decades lying to myself. Which is the comfortable way. Which is the way where Magnús Þorsteinsson is a sensible man surrounded by eccentrics, and the story is a funny one, and nobody has to sit with it afterward.

Elísabet Jónsdóttir was right. About the signal, about its content, about what it meant, and about what had to be done. I am telling you this now because I will spend much of what follows making her sound impossible, and I need you to understand that when I say *impossible* I am describing the limitations of my own imagination and calling them the walls of the world.

She had a word for that. For me. For what I was.

But I'll get there.

---

## II.

The Krafla volcanic system sits in the northeast of Iceland, in that stretch of country where the earth is either frozen or molten and cannot seem to decide between the two. In April of 1971, the Icelandic National Broadcasting Service logged a series of complaints from residents in the Mývatn region about interference on their radio receivers. The interference was not unusual in itself — volcanic activity generates electromagnetic noise, and anyone living near Krafla understood that their reception of *Útvarpið Ríkisins* would occasionally be interrupted by the subsurface opinions of the planet. What was unusual was the pattern. The interference was not random. It occurred at predictable intervals, on specific frequencies, and when the INBS dispatched a technician to investigate, his report noted — in language that I would later recognize as the careful prose of a man trying not to sound insane — that the interference appeared to be *structured.*

I read that report in June. I was at the time employed by the Post and Telephone Administration, working out of the Skúlagata facility in Reykjavik, maintaining the longwave transmission equipment that kept the country's radio service operational. My job was waveforms. I understood them the way a carpenter understands grain — not theoretically but through the hands, through years of contact with the material. I could look at an oscilloscope reading and tell you whether the irregularity was atmospheric, mechanical, or human. I had a reputation for this. I was not modest about it.

Elísabet found me because of that reputation, and because, I suspect, no one else would work with her.

---

She arrived at Skúlagata on a Tuesday, which I remember because Tuesdays were when I performed the weekly calibration of our Rohde & Schwarz EK 07 receiver, and I did not appreciate interruptions to that process. She was perhaps forty, thin-faced, with the particular Icelandic pallor that suggests a person who has been indoors thinking for longer than is medically advisable. She wore a man's coat that did not fit her. She carried a leather briefcase that was older than either of us.

She introduced herself as a physicist attached — loosely, I would learn, very loosely — to the University of Iceland's geophysics program, and she said she needed a radio engineer who could isolate a signal in the 147 to 152 megahertz range emanating from the Krafla caldera, and that the signal was a temporally displaced broadcast from the future.

She said this the way one might say the signal was bouncing off the ionosphere. As a technical detail.

I told her I was in the middle of a calibration.

She sat down on the bench beside the EK 07 and opened her briefcase and removed a sheaf of spectrographic printouts that I recognized as output from a Brüel & Kjær frequency analyzer, and she laid them on my workbench, one after another, in chronological sequence, and she did not say another word for eleven minutes while I looked at them.

I know it was eleven minutes because the EK 07's calibration timer was running and I could hear it ticking.

The printouts showed a signal. It was real — measurably, demonstrably, physically present in the electromagnetic spectrum. It appeared in the VHF band, which was wrong for volcanic noise. It recurred at intervals of approximately 137 minutes, which corresponded to no known geomagnetic cycle. Its waveform was not random. It was, as the INBS technician had carefully noted, *structured.* It bore the unmistakable signature of an amplitude-modulated audio broadcast.

There was a signal coming out of the Krafla volcanic system, on a VHF frequency, and it was shaped like a radio program.

I looked at the printouts for eleven minutes and then I said, "This is interesting."

She said, "It is a broadcast from the future and I can prove it."

I said, "This is an interesting *signal,*" with emphasis.

She looked at me with an expression I would come to know well — the flat, calibrating patience of a woman who has identified the precise boundary of a man's willingness to think and has decided to work around it rather than through it.

"I need your hands," she said. "Not your beliefs."

---

## III.

I want to be precise about why I agreed to help her, because the version where Magnús the sober engineer joins the madwoman's expedition out of secret romantic interest, or hidden adventurousness, or some latent appetite for the impossible, is the version that makes a better story and is not what happened.

What happened was the spectrographs.

The signal was *there.* It was in the data. And it did not belong to any category of electromagnetic phenomenon I had encountered in fourteen years of professional work. Not volcanic noise — wrong frequency band. Not atmospheric skip — wrong propagation pattern. Not military transmission — wrong modulation scheme (I had spent two years monitoring NATO signals during a contract period and knew the signatures). Not a hoax, because the Brüel & Kjær analyzer that had produced the spectrographs was a serious instrument that could not be fooled by a serious person, and Elísabet, whatever I thought of her conclusions, was clearly a serious person.

The signal was a puzzle. I am an engineer. I solve puzzles. That is the whole of it.

I did not believe the signal was a broadcast from the future. I believed it was a genuinely anomalous electromagnetic event with a prosaic explanation that had not yet been identified. My working hypothesis was that a previously undocumented interaction between Krafla's subsurface magmatic chemistry and the region's basalt geology was producing a natural resonance that happened to mimic the structure of an AM broadcast — a geological coincidence, remarkable but not supernatural.

I explained this hypothesis to Elísabet at length, with diagrams. She listened. When I finished, she said — and I am quoting her exactly, because some sentences remain in the memory like splinters — "You have drawn me a very detailed map of a country that does not exist, and the draftsmanship is excellent."

I did not enjoy working with Elísabet Jónsdóttir.

---

## IV.

*I did not enjoy working with her, and I need you to understand that what I am about to describe was not an adventure. I know how it will sound — the misfit team, the improvised equipment, the secret operation. It sounds like the kind of story that is fun to have lived through. But it was not fun while I lived through it. It was tedious and cold and often frightening in the specific way that doing something technically illegal in a small country where everyone knows your name is frightening — not dramatically, but with the steady low-grade nausea of a man who can see his pension evaporating.*

*Sólveig keeps telling me I should explain who was on the team. Sólveig is my granddaughter and she is the one who convinced me to do this. She says I should "set the scene." She grew up watching films where the expert assembles a team and each member has a specialty and a colorful nickname. I will disappoint her.*

---

There were five of us.

Elísabet, who was the reason for everything and who I have described sufficiently for now.

Myself, who was the reason any of the equipment worked.

Guðmundur Halldórsson, a fisherman from Húsavík, whose trawler — the *Njála* — had been partially decommissioned the previous winter after an engine fire, and who was willing to let us strip the vessel's radio equipment in exchange for a sum of money I considered irresponsible and Elísabet considered trivial. She came from money. Old Reykjavik family money, the kind that does not announce itself but is always somehow present when needed. Guðmundur was sixty-one and smelled permanently of cod and diesel, and he had the finest pair of hands I have ever seen on a non-engineer. He could strip and rebuild a marine radio transceiver in the dark, by touch, in a rolling sea. These are not skills you learn. They are skills you are born with and then spend forty years refining, and when I tell you that Guðmundur's hands were as good as mine, I am paying him the highest compliment I know how to offer.

Þórdís Magnúsdóttir, a graduate student in Elísabet's department, who served as our driver, our logistician, and our interface with the world of people who went to sleep at reasonable hours. She was twenty-three, fiercely competent, and treated Elísabet with the particular mixture of worship and exasperation that I associate with bright young women in the orbit of brilliant older women who do not notice they are being worshipped. Þórdís kept a logbook. Her logbook was better organized than mine. This bothered me.

And Haraldur Benediktsson, a bureaucrat in the Icelandic Telecommunications Administration who was, very quietly and very carefully, losing his mind.

Haraldur is the one who requires explanation, because Haraldur was our access point to the frequency allocation records that told us exactly which bands were monitored by whom, and more importantly, which bands were *restricted* — allocated by international agreement to military or governmental use and therefore patrolled. The 147–152 MHz range in which Elísabet's signal appeared fell within a band designated for NATO and Warsaw Pact maritime coordination in the North Atlantic. This meant two things: first, that any sustained monitoring operation on those frequencies by Icelandic civilians would be detected and shut down within days; and second, that other people — professional, state-sponsored, well-equipped people — were already listening to those frequencies and had presumably already noticed the anomalous signal.

Haraldur confirmed this. The Soviets had noticed. They had a monitoring station at Þingvellir — this was not widely known but was one of those open secrets that the Icelandic government preferred to treat as a closed one — and they had logged the Krafla signal as early as February 1971. They had classified it. They had not, as far as Haraldur could determine, identified it.

This was the problem. The signal was real, it was on restricted frequencies, the Soviets knew it existed and were actively monitoring it, and any attempt by our team to capture it with sufficient fidelity for analysis would require sustained access to those same frequencies, which would light up every monitoring station in the North Atlantic like a Christmas display.

Elísabet's solution was to bribe the Soviets.

---

I said this was insane.

She said, "You keep using that word."

I said it was specifically, technically, and legally insane — that bribing Soviet intelligence personnel was a crime against the Icelandic state, a potential violation of NATO security agreements, and the kind of thing that got people put in rooms with no windows.

She said she was not proposing to bribe Soviet intelligence personnel. She was proposing to bribe a technician. There was a difference. Soviet intelligence ran on ideology. Soviet technicians ran on boredom and Western cigarettes and the particular slow-burning desperation of men stationed in Iceland who had expected to be stationed in Cuba.

She had already made contact with the technician. His name was Grigory. He worked the night shift at the Þingvellir facility, and for a total price of four hundred American dollars and twelve cartons of Pall Mall cigarettes, he would designate a six-hour window — 2200 to 0400 on a night of our choosing — during which the Krafla frequencies would be logged as "atmospherically compromised" and excluded from active monitoring.

Six hours. That was what we were buying. Six hours of silence from the people who were listening.

"And if someone in Moscow decides to check the logs?" I said.

"Then Grigory will have a bad week," Elísabet said. "But we will already have what we need."

I asked her if she cared about Grigory.

She said, "I care about what we are going to hear."

---

## V.

*The question Sólveig keeps asking — she is here, behind the camera, she thinks I can't see her mouthing the questions she wants me to answer — is whether I was afraid. She is asking the wrong question. I was not afraid. Fear requires that you believe something dangerous is happening. I did not believe anything dangerous was happening. I believed I was helping a deluded physicist conduct an elaborate exercise in anomaly chasing that would end with a deflating natural explanation and a good story for dinner parties.*

*I was annoyed. That was my condition. Annoyed at the logistics, annoyed at the cold, annoyed at Elísabet's refusal to entertain my geological-resonance hypothesis, annoyed at the discovery that Guðmundur's hands were almost as good as mine. I narrated my own experience to myself as a comedy of inconvenience: the serious engineer tolerating the eccentrics because the puzzle was interesting enough to justify the discomfort.*

*The thing about being annoyed — and I have had forty-eight years to understand this — is that it is the most effective form of not paying attention. Annoyance is a wall you build facing inward. You are so busy cataloging the ways you are being inconvenienced that you do not notice the ways you are being changed.*

---

## VI.

We spent three weeks preparing. I will describe the technical work because it is what I know and because it matters, and because the nature of the equipment we built is part of the story in a way that only becomes clear later.

The *Njála* yielded a Sailor R105 marine receiver, a Skanti TRP-6000 transceiver that Guðmundur had personally modified with an extended VHF capability, and — the real prize — a magnetic tape recorder, a Tandberg Model 64, that some previous owner had installed for reasons Guðmundur could not or would not explain. The Tandberg was beautiful. Four-track stereo, 7.5 inches per second, frequency response flat to 16 kilohertz. It had been exposed to salt air for years and the transport mechanism was corroded, but the heads were intact, and when I rebuilt the tape path with components scavenged from a consumer-grade Philips unit that Þórdís acquired from a student in her department, it ran as smoothly as the day it left the Norwegian factory.

I also built, from a combination of purchased and stolen parts, a directional antenna array specifically tuned to the 147–152 MHz band. The design was a stacked Yagi-Uda, four elements, with a calculated gain of approximately 11 dBi, mounted on a wooden frame that Guðmundur constructed from scrap lumber because we could not afford aluminum. Wooden antenna frames are not standard practice. They work less well than metal. This is the kind of compromise you make when your budget is finite and your physicist refuses to spend money on "scaffolding" when she could spend it on Pall Mall cigarettes for a Soviet technician named Grigory.

Elísabet and I argued about the antenna frame for two days. This is not interesting in itself but it is representative. We argued about everything. We argued about cable impedance matching. We argued about recording levels. We argued about whether to use 3M Scotch 111 tape or BASF LGS 52, a dispute that occupied an entire evening and that she won by producing a technical paper on BASF's superior oxide coating uniformity that I had not read and could not rebut. I argued from experience. She argued from first principles. In retrospect, I understand that she was always arguing from first principles and I was always arguing from the set of things I already knew, and that these are not the same kind of argument, and that one of them is larger than the other.

At the
